claim_verdicts.evidence: JsonValueKind (applies to net-10.0): "Specifies the data type of a JSON value." Fields: Object "A JSON object", Array, String, Number, True "The JSON value true", False, Null "The JSON value null"; the only other field, Undefined, is "There is no value". So .NET 10 knows exactly the seven kinds the lesson lists.

"The JSON format does not directly support dates and times." and "a DateTime type is represented in JSON as a string" (stand-alone-json-serialization.md:56,58). System.Text.Json "parses and writes DateTime and DateTimeOffset values according to the ISO 8601-1:2019 extended profile"; non-conforming text makes JsonSerializer throw (system-text-json-support.md:18,35), i.e. the string format is an agreement.

"The System.Text.Json default is to throw exceptions for comments because the RFC 8259 specification doesn't include them." Probe (.NET 10, default options): deserializing {"a":1 /* c */} -> JsonException.

Docs map "All numeric types, for example Int32, Decimal or Double" to the single JSON type "Number" (stand-alone-json-serialization.md:26). Probe (System.Text.Json, .NET 10): "3" -> int 3 and double 3; "3.5" -> double 3.5, int throws JsonException. The receiving type decides.

The UTF-8 MUST is RFC 8259 §8.1, which is neither a docs root in versions.yaml nor in refs/rfc/. Allowed sources only say UTF-8 "is the most prevalent encoding for data on the web and files on disk" (system-text-json/overview.md:20); no allowed text says JSON between systems must be UTF-8. Grep of refs/aspnetcore-docs for a UTF-8 requirement: no match. Kind fact: D1 not blocked.

Captured output at stage-0: wc -m prints 7, wc -c prints 11, od prints " c4 90 c3 a0 20 4e e1 ba b5 6e 67". Probe: Encoding.UTF8.GetString of those 11 bytes has Length 7, so Đ=c4 90, à=c3 a0, space=20, N=4e, ẵ=e1 ba b5, ng=6e 67.

RFC 9110 §8.6: "The \"Content-Length\" header field indicates the associated representation's data length as a decimal non-negative integer number of octets." Captured output: Content-Length: 40 with body {"id":13,"customer_id":1,"status":"new"}, 40 ASCII characters.

RFC 9110 §8.3: "The \"Content-Type\" header field indicates the media type of the associated representation ... The indicated media type defines both the data format and how that data is intended to be processed by a recipient". ASP.NET Core 10 binding table: "Wrong content type (not application/json) | ... | body | 415", tying JSON bodies to application/json.

RFC 9110 §15.5.16: "the origin server is refusing to service the request because the content is in a format not supported by this method on the target resource. The format problem might be due to the request's indicated Content-Type or Content-Encoding, or as a result of inspecting the data directly."

RFC 9110 §15.5.1: "The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, ...)". ASP.NET Core 10: "Failure to deserialize JSON body | doesn't matter | body | 400".

Probe (.NET 10, Encoding.Latin1.GetString of c4 90 c3 a0 20 4e e1 ba b5 6e 67): 11 chars, one per byte: U+00C4, U+0090 (Control), U+00C3, U+00A0 (SpaceSeparator), U+0020, U+004E, U+00E1, U+00BA, U+00B5, U+006E, U+0067. Đ, à, ẵ give 2, 2, 3 characters, two invisible; e1 ba b5 -> [áºµ]; 4e -> [N].

Verified parts: the capture prints the answer's headers (post-json.txt:2-7) before its body (:9); Caddyfile@stage-0 @postOrder (method POST, path /api/v1/orders) is the only handle answering 201 (:14-17, 36-40). Unverified: that -H sends that header and -d supplies the request body. No curl key in versions.yaml, no curl manual in refs/, `curl --help` denied by permissions, Docker daemon down (no request capture). Kind behavior: D1 not blocked.

"*Serialization* is the process of converting the state of an object, that is, the values of its properties, into a form that can be stored or transmitted ... *Deserialization* reconstructs an object from the serialized form." (overview.md:18); "reading and writing JSON text encoded as UTF-8" (:20); SerializeToUtf8Bytes (how-to.md:88-92). The UTF-8 MUST stays with claim 5.

Execution at stage-0 (captured, CI-checked output): od prints exactly 11 bytes and no 0a, and wc -m prints 7 not 8, so printf '%s' added no line break; wc -c prints 11 (bytes) and wc -m prints 7 (characters in the lab box's locale); od -An -tx1 prints " c4 90 c3 a0 ...": two hex digits per byte, no address column.

Caddyfile@stage-0:14-17 match POST /api/v1/orders; :36-40 header Content-Type "application/json; charset=utf-8", header Location, respond `{"id":13,"customer_id":1,"status":"new"}` 201: a fixed body with no reference to the request body. Captured output shows exactly this answer.

First half verified: RFC 9110 §8.3.2 "HTTP uses \"charset\" names to indicate or negotiate the character encoding scheme ... of a textual representation." Second half (application/json defines no charset parameter; adding one has no effect) is RFC 8259 §11, not reachable from versions.yaml or refs/rfc/. Kind fact: D1 not blocked.

Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- json-round-trip` at stage-0: line 1 {"productId":3,"quantity":2}.

Raw string literals can include whitespace and new lines, embedded quotes, and other special characters. Raw string literals are enclosed in a minimum of three double quotation marks". The sample compiles and runs under net10.0.

Execution at stage-0, last line: "characters: 18, bytes in UTF-8: 22". Docs: "The string.Length property returns the number of char instances in the string instance" and it "doesn't necessarily indicate the number of displayed characters" (character-encoding-introduction.md:21,91). The source text is precomposed (18 chars = 9 + 7 + 2), so here one char per character.

Program.cs@stage-0:16 ["json-round-trip"] = Sync(JsonRoundTrip.Run); :27-38 look up args[0] and await run(). dotnet-run.md:198 `--` "Delimits arguments to dotnet run from arguments for the application being run." Running the command from the repository root printed the four lines the lesson quotes.

Conditional advice, not stated as a rule. The two refusals the docs list for a JSON body are exactly label vs body: ASP.NET Core 10 "Failure to deserialize JSON body ... 400" and "Wrong content type (not application/json) ... 415"; RFC 9110 §15.5.16 names "the request's indicated Content-Type" as a cause of 415.

No allowed document describes how text editors pick an encoding. RFC 9110 §8.3.2 (source_hint) only defines charset names in HTTP fields. Grep of refs/dotnet-docs/docs/standard for encoding detection/guessing: no match. Kind fact: D1 not blocked.

issues.quote: Two programs exchange bytes; to read the values meant, they must agree on format and encoding, and a server checks `Content-Type` and field names.
issues.text: Unlisted claim: "a server checks `Content-Type` and field names" is an unconditional behavior claim with no ledger entry, and the lesson contradicts it: section 5 says the lab "never reads the body", and sections 5-6 show the sample skipping names that match no property and throwing nothing. Read as written, it restates misconception 3 (name mismatch fails loudly). Flagged as minor last round and left unchanged.
issues.fix: Rewrite summary line 1 as: "Two programs exchange bytes; to read the values meant, they must agree on format, encoding and field names, and `Content-Type` names the format." No new claim needed (claims 5, 8, 19 cover it). Update the vi summary to match.

issues.quote: C -->|"sent with Content-Type: application/json"| D["Bytes at the receiver"]
issues.text: Section 4 opens "In the situation above, the order line starts as a C# object inside the sample", and the diagram follows that object through bytes and a Content-Type. JsonRoundTrip.cs sends nothing: Serialize returns a string that goes straight to Deserialize in the same process, and no Content-Type exists anywhere in it. The only Content-Type in the lesson belongs to post-json.sh and a different body (an order, snake_case).
issues.fix: Relabel the C -> D edge (0 words under A.1) to "sent with Content-Type: application/json, between two real programs; the sample skips the wire", or rename node A to "Order line object in a sender" and F to "... in a receiver" so the diagram no longer reads as the sample.

issues.quote: From the same folder, run `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- json-round-trip` and read the last line.
issues.text: Step 2 needs the .NET 10 SDK on the learner's own computer (DonHang.Samples.csproj targets net10.0). STAGE.md@stage-0 says Docker Desktop is "the single prerequisite", and lab/Dockerfile adds only openssl, git, postgresql17-client and procps, so the lab box has no dotnet either. issues.quote: So a date has to go as a string, and reading that string as a date is an agreement between the two programs, not part of JSON.
issues.text: Key (a) is correct. The explanation overstates the lesson: section 4 and section 6 say a date "usually travels as a string"; nothing in the lesson says it must, and a number is also a valid JSON value for it.
issues.fix: In the en explanation `correct`, replace "So a date has to go as a string" with "So a date usually goes as a string"; in vi, replace "ngày phải đi dưới dạng chuỗi" with "ngày thường đi dưới dạng chuỗi".

issues.quote: Caddy answers `201` only to a `POST` on this path.
issues.text: The prose says Caddy answers 201 only to a POST, but the block never says POST: no method appears anywhere in the curl command. I know HTTP methods, so I look for the verb, cannot find it, and cannot tell which part of the command makes this request a POST.

issues.quote: Plain English letters stay the same.
issues.text: The paragraph says a one-byte-per-character encoding turns multi-byte letters into wrong characters, then that plain English letters stay the same. I cannot see why: nothing says ISO-8859-1 reads byte 4e as N, the same letter UTF-8 wrote. Section 5 repeats it ('while `4e` is still `N`') without the reason, and quiz q2 relies on exactly this pattern.
issues.fix: Replace 'Plain English letters stay the same.' with one sentence saying that for plain English letters both encodings use the same single byte, so decoding with the wrong one still gives the right letter.
